final_proof:
Let \(x\in(a,b)\). Since \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), it is Riemann integrable on every subinterval. For every nonzero \(h\) such that \(x+h\in[a,b]\), additivity of the integral gives
\[
F(x+h)-F(x)=\int_a^{x+h}f(t)\,dt-\int_a^x f(t)\,dt
=\int_x^{x+h}f(t)\,dt.
\]
Consequently, using \(\int_x^{x+h}f(x)\,dt=h f(x)\), with the usual orientation convention when \(h<0\),
\[
\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}-f(x)
=\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}\bigl(f(t)-f(x)\bigr)\,dt.
\]

We prove that the right-hand side tends to zero as \(h\to0\). Let \(\varepsilon>0\). By continuity of \(f\) at \(x\), there is \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
|f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon
\]
whenever \(t\in[a,b]\) and \(|t-x|<\delta\). If \(0<|h|<\delta\) and \(x+h\in[a,b]\), every point \(t\) between \(x\) and \(x+h\) satisfies \(|t-x|\le |h|<\delta\). Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left|\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}(f(t)-f(x))\,dt\right|
&\le \frac1{|h|}\int_{\min\{x,x+h\}}^{\max\{x,x+h\}}|f(t)-f(x)|\,dt\\
&\le \frac1{|h|}\varepsilon |h|=\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
F'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}h=f(x).
\]
Since \(x\) was arbitrary, \(F'=f\) throughout \((a,b)\). Hence \(F\) is a primitive of \(f\) on \([a,b]\), under the standard convention that differentiability on a closed interval is required at its interior points.

If derivatives on a closed interval are understood as relative derivatives, the endpoints are also covered: the same estimate with \(h\to0^+\) at \(a\) gives \(F'_+(a)=f(a)\), while the estimate with \(h\to0^-\) at \(b\) gives \(F'_-(b)=f(b)\). Thus the conclusion holds under either convention.
